Small Counterexamples to the Gaussian Moments Conjecture

Christopher D. Long Email: galizur@gmail.com
July 20, 2026
Abstract

We give explicit complex polynomials P,QP,Q in three independent standard real Gaussian variables such that

𝔼⁡(Pm)=0,𝔼⁡(Q​Pm)=m!≠0\mathbb{E}(P^{m})=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}(QP^{m})=m!\neq 0

for every m≥1m\geq 1. In natural complex linear coordinates, PP has five terms and total degree 44. Hence the Gaussian Moments Conjecture is false in every dimension n≥3n\geq 3. We also give a six-term cubic example in four variables, which was found first and already proves failure for every n≥4n\geq 4. Both examples follow from the same coefficient identity. The search was prompted by Levent Alpöge’s public announcement of an explicit three-dimensional counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture. Although the main theorem of Derksen, van den Essen, and Zhao is stated globally in dimension, its proof has fixed-dimensional content: a noninvertible cubic-homogeneous Keller map in rr variables forces the failure of GMC⁡(2​r)\mathrm{GMC}(2r). Tracking a standard Bass–Connell–Wright reduction of the announced map gives a conservative cubic-homogeneous counterexample in 7979 variables, and hence a route-based failure of GMC⁡(158)\mathrm{GMC}(158). That route is nonconstructive at the final Gaussian step and does not furnish explicit polynomials P,QP,Q. The much smaller explicit failures in dimensions 44 and 33 below were not derived from the announced Jacobian map.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 60E05; Secondary 14R15, 05A15.

Keywords. Gaussian Moments Conjecture, Jacobian Conjecture, Gaussian moments, Lagrange inversion.

1 Introduction

Let X=(X1,…,Xn)X=(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}) be a vector of independent standard real Gaussian random variables. Derksen, van den Essen, and Zhao formulated the Gaussian Moments Conjecture GMC⁡(n)\mathrm{GMC}(n) as follows: if P∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]P\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] satisfies

𝔼⁡(P​(X)m)=0(m≥1),\mathbb{E}\bigl(P(X)^{m}\bigr)=0\qquad(m\geq 1),

then, for every Q∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]Q\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}],

𝔼⁡(Q⁡(X)​P​(X)m)=0\mathbb{E}\bigl(Q(X)P(X)^{m}\bigr)=0

for all sufficiently large mm [4, Conjecture 1.1]. Complex coefficients are essential to the formulation: for real coefficients, the condition at m=2m=2 already forces P=0P=0.

The logical relation with the Jacobian Conjecture requires some care. Derksen, van den Essen, and Zhao proved [4, Theorem 1.6] that

(∀n≥1,GMC(n))⟹JC,\bigl(\forall n\geq 1,\ \mathrm{GMC}(n)\bigr)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathrm{JC},

where JC\mathrm{JC} denotes the Jacobian Conjecture in all dimensions. The latter conjecture was proposed by Keller [7]. The contrapositive of this displayed theorem, taken in isolation, gives only

¬JC⟹∃n≥2​ such that ​¬GMC⁡(n),\neg\mathrm{JC}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exists n\geq 2\text{ such that }\neg\mathrm{GMC}(n), (1)

where the restriction n≥2n\geq 2 uses the known truth of GMC⁡(1)\mathrm{GMC}(1) [4, Proposition 4.2].

Fixed-dimensional content of the proof. The proof of the theorem is stronger than its global formulation. Let SIC⁡(r)\mathrm{SIC}(r) denote Zhao’s Special Image Conjecture in rr variables. Propositions 3.2 and 3.1 of [4] give, for each fixed rr,

GMC⁡(2​r)⟹SIC⁡(r).\mathrm{GMC}(2r)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathrm{SIC}(r).

For a fixed cubic-homogeneous Keller map F=z−HF=z-H in rr variables, the proof of [9, Theorem 3.7] shows that SIC⁡(r)\mathrm{SIC}(r) implies that FF is invertible. Consequently,

F=z−H:ℂr⟶ℂr,H​ cubic homogeneous,detJ​F=1,F​ not invertible}⟹¬GMC(2r).\left.\begin{array}[]{c}F=z-H:\mathbb{C}^{r}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}^{r},\\ H\text{ cubic homogeneous},\quad\det JF=1,\\ F\text{ not invertible}\end{array}\right\}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\neg\mathrm{GMC}(2r). (2)

Here J​HJH denotes the Jacobian matrix. This implication identifies a Gaussian dimension after a cubic-homogeneous reduction, but it need not produce explicit Gaussian witness polynomials: Proposition 3.1 of [4] uses a countable-union argument over Zariski-closed sets.

On July 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge publicly announced an explicit three-dimensional counterexample [2]. Kevin Buzzard’s contemporaneous account identifies Akhil as Akhil Mathew, reports that Mathew suggested the problem to Alpöge, and states that the announcement credited Fable with finding the counterexample [3]. Buzzard also records that Paul Lezeau manually formalized the example in Lean; Lezeau submitted the formalization to Google DeepMind’s Formal Conjectures repository [8]. The input dimension 33 does not itself transfer to the index in GMC⁡(n)\mathrm{GMC}(n), but the standard homogeneous reduction can be tracked. Section 2 gives the conservative bound ¬GMC⁡(158)\neg\mathrm{GMC}(158) from this route. The explicit examples presented later are substantially smaller and were not obtained from the announced map.

The first construction gives a cubic counterexample in four real Gaussian variables, proving GMC⁡(n)\mathrm{GMC}(n) false for every n≥4n\geq 4. The second replaces one complex Gaussian pair by one real Gaussian variable and yields a quartic counterexample in three variables. Thus the final conclusion is

GMC⁡(n)​ is false for every ​n≥3.\boxed{\mathrm{GMC}(n)\text{ is false for every }n\geq 3.}

2 A tracked bound from the announced Jacobian map

We record a quantitative consequence because it distinguishes the global statement of [4, Theorem 1.6] from the fixed-dimensional content of its proof. In the normalization used in Lezeau’s formalization [8], the announced map is

F1\displaystyle F_{1} =(1+2​x​y)3​z+4​y2​(1+2​x​y)​(2+3​x​y),\displaystyle=(1+2xy)^{3}z+4y^{2}(1+2xy)(2+3xy),
F2\displaystyle F_{2} =y+3​x​(1+2​x​y)2​z+12​x​y2​(2+3​x​y),\displaystyle=y+3x(1+2xy)^{2}z+12xy^{2}(2+3xy),
F3\displaystyle F_{3} =−x+3​x2​y+x3​z.\displaystyle=-x+3x^{2}y+x^{3}z.

It has Jacobian determinant 11 and identifies the distinct points

(1,−34,134),(−1,34,134).\left(1,-\frac{3}{4},\frac{13}{4}\right),\qquad\left(-1,\frac{3}{4},\frac{13}{4}\right).

Composing on the target with the linear automorphism (u,v,w)↦(−w,v,u)(u,v,w)\mapsto(-w,v,u) gives a normalized map GG with linear part the identity:

G1=\displaystyle G_{1}={} x−3​x2​y−x3​z,\displaystyle x-3x^{2}y-x^{3}z,
G2=\displaystyle G_{2}={} y+3​x​z+24​x​y2+12​x2​y​z+36​x2​y3+12​x3​y2​z,\displaystyle y+3xz+24xy^{2}+12x^{2}yz+36x^{2}y^{3}+12x^{3}y^{2}z,
G3=\displaystyle G_{3}={} z+8​y2+6​x​y​z+28​x​y3+12​x2​y2​z+24​x2​y4+8​x3​y3​z.\displaystyle z+8y^{2}+6xyz+28xy^{3}+12x^{2}y^{2}z+24x^{2}y^{4}+8x^{3}y^{3}z.

Among its terms of degree at least 44, there are respectively 3,2,2,13,2,2,1 monomials of degrees 4,5,6,74,5,6,7.

Proposition 2.1.

The announced three-variable Jacobian counterexample, together with the standard degree and homogeneous reductions, implies ¬GMC⁡(158)\neg\mathrm{GMC}(158).

Proof.

We track the elementary reduction in [1, Section 3]. Let c⁡(d)c(d) be an upper bound for the number of degree-lowering steps required for one monomial of degree dd, with c⁡(d)=0c(d)=0 for d≤3d\leq 3. If a degree-dd monomial is factored as P​QPQ, where deg⁡P=p\deg P=p, deg⁡Q=q\deg Q=q, p+q=dp+q=d, and p,q≤d−2p,q\leq d-2, one Bass–Connell–Wright step adds two variables and replaces it by terms of degrees at most

p+1,q+1,p,q,2.p+1,\quad q+1,\quad p,\quad q,\quad 2.

Thus

c⁡(d)≤1+c⁡(p+1)+c⁡(q+1)+c⁡(p)+c⁡(q).c(d)\leq 1+c(p+1)+c(q+1)+c(p)+c(q).

Using the balanced choices 4=2+24=2+2, 5=2+35=2+3, 6=3+36=3+3, and 7=3+47=3+4 gives

c⁡(4)=1,c⁡(5)≤2,c⁡(6)≤3,c⁡(7)≤5.c(4)=1,\qquad c(5)\leq 2,\qquad c(6)\leq 3,\qquad c(7)\leq 5.

The displayed support of GG therefore requires at most

3​c​(4)+2​c​(5)+2​c​(6)+c⁡(7)≤183c(4)+2c(5)+2c(6)+c(7)\leq 18

steps. Since each step adds two variables, this produces a noninvertible Keller map of degree at most 33 with identity linear part in

s=3+2⋅18=39s=3+2\cdot 18=39

variables.

For completeness, the next dimension count can be read directly from the construction in [1, Section 4]; its optional multilinearization is not needed here. Write the resulting map as

K⁡(X)=X+K(2)​(X)+K(3)​(X),X∈ℂs.K(X)=X+K^{(2)}(X)+K^{(3)}(X),\qquad X\in\mathbb{C}^{s}.

In variables (X,Y)∈ℂ2​s(X,Y)\in\mathbb{C}^{2s}, the map

U⁡(X,Y)=(X+K(2)​(X)+Y,Y−K(3)​(X))U(X,Y)=\bigl(X+K^{(2)}(X)+Y,\;Y-K^{(3)}(X)\bigr)

is stably equivalent to KK, has the form (X,Y)+N⁡(X,Y)(X,Y)+N(X,Y) with deg⁡N≤3\deg N\leq 3, and has nilpotent J​NJN. One direct verification uses

Et​(X)=X+t​K(2)​(X)+t2​K(3)​(X)E_{t}(X)=X+tK^{(2)}(X)+t^{2}K^{(3)}(X)

and observes that (X,Y)+t​N(X,Y)+tN is obtained from the stabilization of EtE_{t} by elementary pre- and post-compositions. Hence I+t​J​NI+tJN is invertible over the polynomial ring in tt, which forces J​NJN to be nilpotent. Finally, the Bass–Connell–Wright homogenization adds one variable and replaces the degree-11, 22, and 33 parts of NN by

N(1)​T2+N(2)​T+N(3).N^{(1)}T^{2}+N^{(2)}T+N^{(3)}.

This gives a noninvertible map equal to the identity plus a cubic-homogeneous map in

r=2​s+1=79r=2s+1=79

variables. Applying (2) gives ¬GMC⁡(2​r)=¬GMC⁡(158)\neg\mathrm{GMC}(2r)=\neg\mathrm{GMC}(158). ∎

Remark 2.2.

The number 158158 is a transparent upper bound, not an optimization and not a claim about the least failing Gaussian dimension. The reduction depends on the degree and monomial support of the particular Jacobian map; it does not give a bound depending only on the original input dimension 33. It also does not supply explicit Gaussian witness polynomials P,QP,Q.

3 Gaussian contractions

Let X,YX,Y be independent standard real Gaussians and put

Z=X+i​Y2,W=X−i​Y2.Z=\frac{X+iY}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad W=\frac{X-iY}{\sqrt{2}}.

Then W=Z¯W=\overline{Z} as random variables, while both are complex linear polynomials in X,YX,Y. Rotational invariance gives

𝔼⁡(Wa​Zb)=δa​b​a!(a,b≥0).\mathbb{E}(W^{a}Z^{b})=\delta_{ab}\,a!\qquad(a,b\geq 0). (3)

Equivalently, for every polynomial R∈ℂ⁡[z]R\in\mathbb{C}[z],

𝔼⁡(Wa​R​(Z))=a!​[za]​R​(z).\mathbb{E}\bigl(W^{a}R(Z)\bigr)=a!\,[z^{a}]R(z). (4)

If TT is an independent standard real Gaussian, then

𝔼⁡(T2​k)=(2​k−1)!!=(2​k)!2k​k!,\mathbb{E}(T^{2k})=(2k-1)!!=\frac{(2k)!}{2^{k}k!}, (5)

and hence, as a formal ordinary generating function,

∑k≥0(−1)k4k(2​kk)uk=(1+u)−1/2.\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{4^{k}}\binom{2k}{k}u^{k}=(1+u)^{-1/2}. (6)

All exponential generating functions below are formal identities; no analytic integrability of et​Pe^{tP} is asserted or needed.

Z=X1+i​X22,W=X1−i​X22.Z=\frac{X_{1}+iX_{2}}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad W=\frac{X_{1}-iX_{2}}{\sqrt{2}}.

Define

P3=(1+Z)​(W−12​(2+Z)​T2)=W+WZ−T2−32ZT2−12Z2T2,Q3=Z.\begin{split}P_{3}&=(1+Z)\left(W-\frac{1}{2}(2+Z)T^{2}\right)\\ &=W+WZ-T^{2}-\frac{3}{2}ZT^{2}-\frac{1}{2}Z^{2}T^{2},\qquad Q_{3}=Z.\end{split} (10)

Thus P3P_{3} has five terms and total degree 44.

For every A∈ℂ⁡[z]A\in\mathbb{C}[z] and m≥1m\geq 1,

𝔼⁡(A⁡(Z)​P3m)=m!​[zm]​A​(z)​(1+z)m−1.\mathbb{E}\bigl(A(Z)P_{3}^{m}\bigr)=m!\,[z^{m}]A(z)(1+z)^{m-1}. (11)

𝔼(P3m)=0,𝔼(Q3P3m)=m!≠0(m≥1).\mathbb{E}(P_{3}^{m})=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}(Q_{3}P_{3}^{m})=m!\neq 0\qquad(m\geq 1). (12)

Write

h⁡(z)=1+z,v⁡(z)=−12​(1+z)​(2+z),h(z)=1+z,\qquad v(z)=-\frac{1}{2}(1+z)(2+z),

so that P3=W​h​(Z)+v⁡(Z)​T2P_{3}=Wh(Z)+v(Z)T^{2}. Expanding according to the number kk of factors chosen from v⁡(Z)​T2v(Z)T^{2}, and using (4) and (5), gives

=[zm]​A​(z)​(1+z)m​∑k≥0(−1)k4k​(2​kk)​(z⁡(2+z))k.\displaystyle=[z^{m}]A(z)(1+z)^{m}\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{4^{k}}\binom{2k}{k}\bigl(z(2+z)\bigr)^{k}.

1+z⁡(2+z)=(1+z)2,1+z(2+z)=(1+z)^{2},

[zm]A(z)(1+z)m((1+z)2)−1/2=[zm]A(z)(1+z)m−1,[z^{m}]A(z)(1+z)^{m}\bigl((1+z)^{2}\bigr)^{-1/2}=[z^{m}]A(z)(1+z)^{m-1},

Thus

𝔼⁡(et​P3)=1,𝔼⁡(Q3​et​P3)=t1−t.\mathbb{E}(e^{tP_{3}})=1,\qquad\mathbb{E}(Q_{3}e^{tP_{3}})=\frac{t}{1-t}. (13)

The failure of eventual vanishing is maximal: the mixed moment is nonzero for every positive exponent.

Corollary 5.2.

The Gaussian Moments Conjecture GMC⁡(n)\mathrm{GMC}(n) is false for every n≥3n\geq 3.

Proof.

Theorem 5.1 disproves GMC⁡(3)\mathrm{GMC}(3). For n>3n>3, use the same polynomials in the first three variables and ignore the remaining independent Gaussian variables. ∎

Derksen, van den Essen, and Zhao proved GMC⁡(1)\mathrm{GMC}(1) [4, Proposition 4.2]. The only remaining dimension is therefore n=2n=2.

6 How the examples were found

The four-variable example arose from the complex-Gaussian realization in [4, Proposition 3.2]. Let Z1,…,ZdZ_{1},\dots,Z_{d} be independent standard circular complex Gaussians and put Wj=Zj¯W_{j}=\overline{Z_{j}}. For a polynomial map H=(H1,…,Hd)H=(H_{1},\dots,H_{d}), consider

P=W⋅H⁡(Z)=∑j=1dWj​Hj​(Z).P=W\mathbin{\cdot}H(Z)=\sum_{j=1}^{d}W_{j}H_{j}(Z).

A form of Lagrange–Good inversion [6] gives

𝔼⁡(A⁡(Z)​et​P)=A⁡(𝒈⁡(t))det(I−t​J​H​(𝒈⁡(t))),𝒈⁡(t)=t​H​(𝒈⁡(t)),\mathbb{E}\bigl(A(Z)e^{tP}\bigr)=\frac{A(\boldsymbol{g}(t))}{\det\bigl(I-tJH(\boldsymbol{g}(t))\bigr)},\qquad\boldsymbol{g}(t)=tH(\boldsymbol{g}(t)), (14)

where J​HJH is the Jacobian matrix and 𝒈⁡(t)∈t​ℂ​[[t]]d\boldsymbol{g}(t)\in t\mathbb{C}[[t]]^{d} is the unique formal solution. The search therefore became: make 𝒈⁡(t)\boldsymbol{g}(t) nonpolynomial, but force the determinant in (14) to equal 11 along this inverse branch. The choice

H1​(z1,z2)=(1−z1)​(1+z2),H2​(z1,z2)=1+z2H_{1}(z_{1},z_{2})=(1-z_{1})(1+z_{2}),\qquad H_{2}(z_{1},z_{2})=1+z_{2}

gives

𝒈⁡(t)=(t,t1−t),det(I−t​J​H​(g⁡(t)))=1.\boldsymbol{g}(t)=\left(t,\frac{t}{1-t}\right),\qquad\det\bigl(I-tJH(g(t))\bigr)=1.

This is precisely P4P_{4}, and A⁡(z1,z2)=z2A(z_{1},z_{2})=z_{2} reads off t/(1−t)t/(1-t).

The three-variable example replaces one circular complex Gaussian pair by one real Gaussian direction. For

P=W​h​(Z)+v⁡(Z)​T2,P=Wh(Z)+v(Z)T^{2},

univariate Lagrange inversion and the identity 𝔼(es​T2)=(1−2s)−1/2\mathbb{E}(e^{sT^{2}})=(1-2s)^{-1/2} give

𝔼⁡(A⁡(Z)​et​P)=A(ζ(t))(1−2tv(ζ(t)))−1/21−t​h′​(ζ⁡(t)),ζ⁡(t)=t​h​(ζ⁡(t)).\mathbb{E}\bigl(A(Z)e^{tP}\bigr)=\frac{A(\zeta(t))\bigl(1-2tv(\zeta(t))\bigr)^{-1/2}}{1-th^{\prime}(\zeta(t))},\qquad\zeta(t)=th(\zeta(t)). (15)

Taking h⁡(z)=1+zh(z)=1+z gives ζ=t/(1−t)\zeta=t/(1-t) and denominator 1−t1-t. The choice

v⁡(z)=−12​(1+z)​(2+z)v(z)=-\frac{1}{2}(1+z)(2+z)

forces

1−2​t​v​(ζ⁡(t))=(1−t)−2,1-2tv(\zeta(t))=(1-t)^{-2},

so the square-root factor is 1−t1-t and cancels the denominator. This yields P3P_{3}. Informally, a single real Gaussian supplies half of the determinant correction supplied by a circular complex pair.

The announced Jacobian counterexample supplied the initial motivation. As Proposition 2.1 records, tracking the known reduction gives the fixed-dimensional but nonexplicit conclusion ¬GMC⁡(158)\neg\mathrm{GMC}(158). The much stronger conclusions ¬GMC⁡(4)\neg\mathrm{GMC}(4) and ¬GMC⁡(3)\neg\mathrm{GMC}(3) come instead from the explicit polynomials above. No coordinate, term, or algebraic feature of the announced map was used in either construction.

7 A brief remark on dimension two

Let Z=(X+i​Y)/2Z=(X+iY)/\sqrt{2}, W=(X−i​Y)/2W=(X-iY)/\sqrt{2}, and U=Z​WU=ZW. Give ZZ weight 11 and WW weight −1-1. Gaussian expectation kills all nonzero weights, while on ℂ⁡[U]\mathbb{C}[U] it is the linear factorial functional ℒ:ℂ⁡[U]→ℂ\mathcal{L}:\mathbb{C}[U]\to\mathbb{C} defined by ℒ⁡(Uj)=j!\mathcal{L}(U^{j})=j!.

This immediately excludes several natural sources of a two-dimensional counterexample. Polynomials supported only on positive weights or only on negative weights satisfy the desired eventual vanishing by weight. Homogeneous polynomials are covered by [4, Corollary 4.4], using the theorem of Duistermaat and van der Kallen [5]. On ℂ⁡[U]\mathbb{C}[U], the hypothesis ℒ⁡(Pm)=0\mathcal{L}(P^{m})=0 for all mm forces P=0P=0 by the one-variable Factorial Conjecture [10, Theorem 4.9]. More generally, if

P=Z​A​(U)+W​B​(U),P=ZA(U)+WB(U),

then odd moments vanish by weight and

𝔼⁡(P2​r)=(2​rr)​ℒ​((U​A​(U)​B​(U))r).\mathbb{E}(P^{2r})=\binom{2r}{r}\mathcal{L}\bigl((UA(U)B(U))^{r}\bigr).

The same theorem forces A=0A=0 or B=0B=0, reducing again to one-sided weights. Thus any counterexample to GMC⁡(2)\mathrm{GMC}(2) would require a richer inhomogeneous mixture of positive and negative weights. We do not settle this case.

AI provenance and author responsibility

The four-variable construction was produced by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Pro, without human intervention after the initial prompt, after it was told that the Jacobian Conjecture had been disproved and asked whether a small counterexample to the Gaussian Moments Conjecture might therefore exist. After being shown the four-variable example, Claude Fable 5 found the three-variable construction and supplied independent algebraic checks and structural comments.
